opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back, my early research wasn't labeled "embodied intelligence" at the time, but the questions were the same ones I work on now.

I started in 3D vision and geometry. During my PhD, a lot of my work was on understanding objects in three dimensions: not just recognizing that something is a mug, but knowing where it is, how it's oriented, how big it is, and what its shape looks like, even if I've never seen that particular mug before. One line of work was category-level object pose estimation. Instead of memorizing one exact CAD model, you learn a normalized, canonical representation for a whole category, so a new instance can be mapped into that shared space.

That might sound like a pure vision problem, but it's really a robotics problem in disguise. If a robot wants to pick up a cup, pour water, or open a drawer, a 2D label isn't enough. It needs a 3D, actionable understanding of the object: where the handle is, which way it faces, how it moves. So that early work was about building the perception that action needs.

The second connection is generalization. In robotics the biggest gap has always been that things work in the lab on a few objects and then fail in a new home or with a new object. Category-level thinking is a form of generalization, finding structure that transfers across instances. That's exactly the core challenge of embodied intelligence today: how do you get a robot to handle the open world, not just a curated demo?

The third thread is data. Very early I realized that real-world 3D and interaction data is extremely expensive to collect. So we leaned heavily on synthetic data and simulation, generating large amounts of labeled data and then figuring out how to bridge the sim-to-real gap. That conviction carried straight into my later work on dexterous grasping and manipulation, where we generate huge numbers of grasps in simulation and train policies that transfer to real robots. I still believe this: for embodied AI, we can't wait for internet-scale robot data to appear. Simulation and synthetic data are a key lever, combined with a smaller amount of high-quality real data.

So the through-line is that I went from "how does a machine see the 3D world" to "how does a machine act in the 3D world." Perception, generalization, and scalable data were the foundations I was building early on, and embodied intelligence is where they all have to come together, because a robot can't just understand. It has to do something, and the physical world tells you very quickly whether your understanding was right.

r001.rationale: The response links perception to action, but does not identify a perception–action loop as the core of embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss predicting a person's next action or a robot proactively accommodating that person.

r003.rationale: It mentions understanding an object's pose and how it moves, but does not identify tracking its precise motion state as a central visual problem in robot interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, my early work was almost entirely about perception. During my PhD at Stanford, most of what I did was 3D vision: understanding point clouds, estimating object poses, learning representations of shapes and scenes. At the time I did not frame it as embodied intelligence. I framed it as teaching a machine to see the three-dimensional world the way we do.

But the connection became obvious once I started asking what the perception was for. If you want an agent to pick up a cup, you need to know where the cup is, how it is oriented, and where the handle is relative to the body of the cup. Category-level 6D pose estimation, which was one of the problems I spent a lot of time on, is exactly that question. It is not about recognizing that something is a cup. It is about giving a robot the geometric information it would need to interact with the cup.

So I would say the early research was building the sensory side of embodiment before I was explicitly working on the body. What changed later was realizing that perception alone is not the hard part. The hard part is closing the loop. A robot's vision system has to be good enough to support action, and the action has to generate the kind of data that makes the vision better. Articulated objects, for example, taught me this. You cannot really understand how a drawer opens just by looking at it. You have to pull it.

That is where I moved from pure 3D vision toward manipulation, and toward learning from interaction. The core problem of embodied intelligence, as I see it now, is that understanding and acting are not two separate modules. My early work gave me the tools to describe the world precisely. The later work is about letting the agent use those descriptions, and update them, through its own actions.

r001.rationale: The response calls closing the loop the hard part and says understanding and acting are not separate modules, identifying the perception–action loop as central.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss predicting a person's next action or a robot proactively accommodating that person.

r003.rationale: It discusses object pose and geometry for interaction, but does not identify tracking an object's precise motion state as a central visual problem.

astra-6.text:
I see a fairly direct connection. My early research focused on understanding 3D environments and how an agent can act within them. Those are also central questions in embodied intelligence: What is around me? What can I do with it? And how will the world change when I act?

For example, recognizing an object is only part of the problem. If a robot wants to pick it up, it needs to understand its geometry, estimate its pose, and find a grasp that will actually work. Then it has to deal with uncertainty—its view may be incomplete, or the object may move during contact.

So the connection is through moving from perception toward interaction. You want representations that help an agent make decisions and act successfully. That brings perception, learning, and control together, which is how I think about the core challenge of embodied intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes perception leading to decisions and action, including how the world changes when the agent acts, and presents this integration as central to embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss predicting a person's next action or a robot proactively accommodating that person.

r003.rationale: It mentions that an object may move during contact, but does not identify tracking its precise motion state as a central visual problem in robot interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the connection through a basic question: how does an intelligent system understand the physical world well enough to act in it? For embodied intelligence, perception is only part of the problem. An agent also needs to understand what its actions might change, what constraints the environment imposes, and how to adapt when its predictions are wrong.

That is the lens through which I would connect my early research to embodied intelligence. Even when you study a narrower problem, the larger challenge is to build representations that are useful for interaction. Recognizing an object is one thing; knowing how to grasp it, move it, or use it requires a different level of understanding.

What makes this particularly interesting is the feedback loop. You perceive, you act, and the result gives you new information. So the goal is not simply a better model of a static scene, but a system that can keep learning through its interaction with the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes the perceive–act–learn feedback loop and presents interaction as central to embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss predicting a person's next action or using that prediction to accommodate them proactively.

r003.rationale: It does not identify precise tracking of an object's motion state as a central visual problem.
